learn.hook: A priest needed a fire altar with exactly twice the area of a square one. Doubling the side gave 4 times the area! Baudhayana found the clever fix.
points: Doubling the side does not double a square: a square of side 2a has area 4a², four times as big.
Baudhayana's Śulba-sūtra method: the square drawn on the diagonal of a square has exactly double its area.
Why: the two diagonals cut the square into 4 congruent right triangles. The square on the diagonal is made of 8 of the same triangles — twice as many.
Paper version: cut two equal squares along their diagonals into 8 triangles, and arrange all 8 into one big square — double the area.
Halving a square: join the midpoints of its sides. The four corner triangles are congruent to the four triangles inside the new square, so the new square has half the area.

example.q: A square has side 3 cm. Make a square with double its area.
steps: Draw the square on its diagonal
(Its side is the diagonal, about 4.24 cm, not 6 cm)
example.answer: Square on the diagonal, area 18 cm²

learn.reallife: Ancient Indian altar builders used rope and pegs to double squares exactly, long before calculators.

learn.hook: Draw a triangle with two sides of 1 cm and a right angle between them. The third side is √2 cm — a number whose decimals never end and never repeat!
points: An isosceles right triangle with legs 1 has hypotenuse c with c² = 1² + 1² = 2, so c = √2.
√2 has no terminating decimal: a decimal with k decimal places, squared, has 2k decimal places ending in a non-zero digit, so it can never equal exactly 2.
√2 is not a fraction p/q: if it were (in lowest terms), then p² = 2q², so p is even; then q² = 2 × (p/2)², so q is even too — impossible for lowest terms. √2 is irrational.
For legs a, the hypotenuse is a√2. Legs 5 give hypotenuse √50 ≈ 7.07, between 7 and 8 since 49 < 50 < 64.

example.q: Between which two numbers with 2 decimal places does √2 lie?

learn.reallife: A4 paper is cut so that its long side ÷ short side ≈ √2 — fold it in half and the shape stays the same!

teach.nudge: What do you get if you square 1.4? Is it exactly 2?

learn.hook: More than 2500 years ago, the Indian mathematician Baudhayana wrote down a rule for building fire altars that we still use to find distances today!
points: A right triangle has one angle of 90°. The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse, and it is the longest side.
The Baudhayana–Pythagoras theorem: if the legs are a and b and the hypotenuse is c, then a² + b² = c².
In Baudhayana's words (roughly): the diagonal of a rectangle makes a square as big as the squares on its length and breadth put together.
To find the hypotenuse: c = √(a² + b²). To find a leg: a = √(c² − b²).
Converse: if the sides of a triangle satisfy a² + b² = c², then the angle opposite c is a right angle.

example.q: A 13 m ladder leans against a wall. Its foot is 5 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
steps: The ladder is the hypotenuse: c = 13
One leg is 5, let the height be h

learn.reallife: Firefighters placing ladders, TV makers measuring screen size along the diagonal, and pilots finding straight-line distances all use this theorem.

quiz.explain: The ladder is the hypotenuse. Height² = 13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144, so the height is 12 m.

= 100 cm² (the side is 10 cm, but the area is 100 cm²).

topics.title: Proof ideas and using the converse

learn.hook: Can you prove a² + b² = c² with just four paper triangles and a square? Yes, with a cut-and-arrange trick!
points: Area proof: draw a big square of side (a + b). Put 4 copies of the right triangle in its corners. The space left in the middle is a tilted square of side c.
Big square area = 4 triangles + middle square: (a + b)² = 4 × ½ab + c². So a² + 2ab + b² = 2ab + c², which gives a² + b² = c².
Rearrangement: slide the same 4 triangles into a different position in the big square, and the space left is two squares, a² and b². Same leftover area, so a² + b² = c².
Baudhayana used the diagonal to double a square: the square on the diagonal of a square has twice its area.
Converse in action: if the longest side c gives a² + b² = c², the triangle is right-angled. If a² + b² > c² it is acute; if a² + b² < c² it is obtuse.

example.q: Use the area proof with a = 3 and b = 4 to find c.

learn.reallife: Masons mark a perfect right angle for a house corner with a knotted rope stretched into a 3-4-5 triangle.

games.title: Right or not?
items: A triangle with sides 6, 8 and 10 has a right angle.
A triangle with sides 4, 5 and 6 has a right angle.
16 + 25 = 41, but 6² = 36. It is an acute triangle.
The diagonal of a square with side 1 has length √2.
In every triangle, a² + b² = c².
This is true only for right triangles.
A knotted rope with sides 3, 4 and 5 units can be used to mark a right angle.
3² + 4² = 5², so by the converse the angle between 3 and 4 is 90°.
If both legs of a right triangle are doubled, the hypotenuse also doubles.

quiz.q: In the area proof, a big square of side (a + b) holds 4 right triangles with legs a and b, and a middle square of side c. If a = 3 and b = 4, what is the area of the middle square?
quiz.explain: Big square = 7² = 49. Four triangles = 4 × 6 = 24. Middle square = 49 − 24 = 25, so c = 5.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract the triangles, or uses only one triangle

quiz.q: A triangle has sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 8 cm. What kind of triangle is it?
quiz.explain: 5² + 6² = 61, which is less than 8² = 64. When the two smaller squares add to less than the largest square, the triangle is obtuse.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any triangle with whole-number sides is right-angled

quiz.q: What is the diagonal of a square of side 5 cm? (Use √2 ≈ 1.41.)
quiz.mistake: Adds the two sides (10 cm) instead of using the theorem

quiz.q: Baudhayana's idea: a square is drawn on the diagonal of a square of side 6 cm. What is the area of the new square?
quiz.explain: Diagonal² = 6² + 6² = 72. The new square's area is diagonal², which is 72 cm², twice the original 36 cm².
quiz.mistake: Doubles the side (12 cm), which makes 144 cm², four times the area

quiz.q: Why do masons use a knotted rope with sides 3, 4 and 5 units?
options: Because 3² + 4² = 5², so the triangle has a right angle for making square corners
Because it makes an equilateral triangle
Because ropes cannot make other shapes
quiz.explain: By the converse of the theorem, sides 3, 4, 5 must make a right angle between the 3 and 4 sides.
steps: By the converse of the theorem, the angle between the 3 and 4 sides is 90°.
So the rope makes a right angle for square corners.
Answer: Because 3² + 4² = 5², so the triangle has a right angle for making square corners
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the converse of the theorem to real right angles

quiz.q: A triangle has sides 9, 10 and 12. Is it acute, right or obtuse?
quiz.explain: 9² + 10² = 181, which is more than 12² = 144. When the two smaller squares add to more than the largest, all angles are acute.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which way the inequality points to acute or obtuse

quiz.q: A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. If both legs are doubled, what is the new hypotenuse?
quiz.explain: The old hypotenuse is 13. Doubling both legs doubles the hypotenuse: 26. Check: 10² + 24² = 676 = 26².
quiz.mistake: Thinks the hypotenuse stays the same or becomes 4 times bigger

quiz.q: In the rearrangement proof, the four triangles are moved inside the same big square so that two squares are left uncovered. What are their areas?
quiz.explain: The leftover space is a square of side a and a square of side b. Before the move it was one square of side c, so a² + b² = c².
steps: The big square and the four triangles are the same before and after the move.
After the move, the uncovered space is a square of side a and a square of side b.
So the areas are a² and b² (and a² + b² = c²).
quiz.mistake: Confuses the triangles' areas (½ab) with the leftover squares

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How does putting 4 triangles inside a big square prove a² + b² = c²?
teach.praise: The leftover space is c² in one arrangement and a² + b² in the other. Same space, so they are equal. Mind blown!
teach.nudge: What is left uncovered in the middle? And what is left after you move the triangles?

topics.title: Combining squares and drawing squares of any area

learn.hook: Can you cut a 3 × 3 and a 4 × 4 square of paper and rebuild them into ONE square? Yes — a 5 × 5 one! That's the theorem in your hands.
points: Two squares with sides a and b can be cut and rearranged into one square of side c, where c² = a² + b². For 3 and 4, c = 5.
To draw a square with 5 times the area of a unit square: draw a right triangle with legs 1 and 2. Its hypotenuse is √5, so the square on it has area 5.
For 3 times the area: use legs 1 and √2 (the diagonal of the unit square). The hypotenuse is √3.
On a square dot grid, a tilted square whose side goes 'a across and b up' has area a² + b². So areas 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10 ... are possible, but area 3 is not (3 is not a sum of two squares).

example.q: Draw a square of area 5 on a dot grid.
steps: Draw a side going 2 across and 1 up
Turn 90° and repeat to make the other sides

learn.reallife: Tile setters and quilt makers combine and tilt squares to fit odd-sized floors and patterns.

learn.hook: 3, 4, 5 is a magic trio: 9 + 16 = 25. Are there more such trios? Infinitely many!
points: A Pythagorean triple is three whole numbers a, b, c with a² + b² = c². The smallest is (3, 4, 5).
Multiply a triple by any whole number to get another: (6, 8, 10), (9, 12, 15), (30, 40, 50).
Some triples are not multiples of smaller ones: (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25), (20, 21, 29).
A recipe: for any whole number m > 1, the numbers 2m, m² − 1 and m² + 1 form a triple. For m = 4: 8, 15, 17.
To test a triple, square the two smaller numbers, add them, and compare with the square of the largest.
learn.reallife: Carpenters and tile layers use triples like 6-8-10 to check that corners are truly square.

topics.title: Primitive triples and Fermat's famous puzzle

learn.hook: a² + b² = c² has endless whole-number answers. But try a³ + b³ = c³ — there are NONE. It took 350 years to prove!
points: A triple is primitive if its three numbers share no common factor bigger than 1: (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17). (6, 8, 10) is not primitive — it is 2 × (3, 4, 5).
Odd-number recipe: n² = 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n − 1). If the last odd number 2n − 1 is itself a square k², then n² = (n − 1)² + k².
Examples: 2n − 1 = 9 gives n = 5 and 5² = 4² + 3²; 2n − 1 = 25 gives 13² = 12² + 5²; 2n − 1 = 49 gives 25² = 24² + 7².
Fermat's Last Theorem: there are no positive whole numbers x, y, z with xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ when n is bigger than 2.
Pierre de Fermat wrote this in the margin of a book (around 1637), saying the margin was too small for his proof. Andrew Wiles finally proved it in 1994.

example.q: Use the odd-number recipe with the odd square 81.

learn.reallife: Mathematicians worked on Fermat's puzzle for over 350 years — proof that some questions are worth a lifetime!

quiz.q: Which of these is a primitive triple?
quiz.explain: 8, 15 and 17 have no common factor above 1. The others are multiples of (3, 4, 5) or (5, 12, 13).
steps: A primitive triple has no common factor bigger than 1.
8, 15, 17 share no factor above 1, so (8, 15, 17) is primitive.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every triple is primitive

quiz.q: (12, 16, 20) is a triple. Dividing by the HCF of its numbers gives which primitive triple?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 2 only

quiz.q: In the odd-number recipe, the odd square 2n − 1 = 25. What is n?
quiz.explain: 2n − 1 = 25 gives n = 13, and then 13² = 12² + 5².
quiz.mistake: Takes the square root of 25 instead

quiz.q: Which triple does the odd square 49 give in the recipe?
quiz.explain: 2n − 1 = 49 gives n = 25, so 25² = 24² + 7²: the triple is (7, 24, 25).
quiz.mistake: Uses 49 itself as a side

quiz.q: The odd square 81 gives a triple. What is its largest number?
quiz.explain: 2n − 1 = 81 gives n = 41, and 41² = 40² + 9².
quiz.mistake: Gives n − 1 instead of n

quiz.q: How many solutions in positive whole numbers does x³ + y³ = z³ have?
quiz.explain: Fermat's Last Theorem (proved by Wiles) says there are none for any power bigger than 2.

Here n = 3, which is bigger than 2.

quiz.explain: Fermat only claimed a proof; Andrew Wiles proved it in 1994.

revise.summary: A primitive triple has no common factor above 1. The odd-number recipe turns an odd square 2n − 1 = k² into n² = (n − 1)² + k². Fermat claimed xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ has no solutions for n > 2, and Andrew Wiles proved it in 1994.

topics.title: More uses: lotus, rhombus, triangles and a box puzzle

learn.hook: In Bhaskara's Lilavati, a lotus sways in the wind until its flower touches the water. From that, you can find how deep the lake is!
points: Lotus problem: a lotus stands h above the water; the wind pushes it until the flower touches the water a distance s away. If the depth is d, the stem is d + h, so d² + s² = (d + h)².
With h = 10 cm and s = 30 cm: d² + 900 = d² + 20d + 100, so 20d = 800 and d = 40 cm.
A rhombus's diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so side² = (half of one diagonal)² + (half of the other)². Diagonals 16 and 12 give side √(8² + 6²) = 10.
An equilateral triangle of side a has altitude h with h² + (a/2)² = a², so h = (√3/2)a. Area = ½ × a × h. For a = 10 cm: h ≈ 8.66 cm and area ≈ 43.3 cm².
Logic puzzle: three boxes are labelled Red, Blue and Mixed, but every label is wrong. Pick one ball from the box labelled Mixed — it can only be all one colour — and you can then work out every box.

example.q: A lotus flower is 10 cm above the water. Pushed by the wind, it touches the water 30 cm away. How deep is the water?

learn.reallife: Engineers use the same theorem to find heights, depths and diagonal braces in buildings and bridges.

games.title: Solve the box puzzle
items: All three labels are wrong
Take one ball from the box labelled Mixed
That box holds only that ball's colour
The box labelled with the other colour must be Mixed
The last box gets the remaining colour

quiz.q: A lotus flower is 10 cm above the water. The wind pushes it until it touches the water 30 cm away. How deep is the water?
quiz.mistake: Takes the stem length (50 cm) as the depth

quiz.q: A lotus flower is 20 cm above the water and touches the water 60 cm away when pushed. How deep is the water?
quiz.mistake: Gives the stem length instead of the depth

quiz.q: A rhombus has diagonals 16 cm and 12 cm. How long is each side?
quiz.explain: Half-diagonals are 8 and 6, and they meet at 90°. Side = √(64 + 36) = 10 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the full diagonals in the theorem

quiz.q: A rhombus has diagonals 10 cm and 24 cm. What is its perimeter?
quiz.explain: Side = √(5² + 12²) = 13 cm, so the perimeter is 4 × 13 = 52 cm.
quiz.mistake: Stops at one side

quiz.q: An equilateral triangle has side 10 cm. Using √3 ≈ 1.732, how long is its altitude?
quiz.mistake: Uses half the side as the altitude

quiz.q: Using an altitude of 8.66 cm, what is the area of an equilateral triangle with side 10 cm?
quiz.explain: Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 10 × 8.66 = 43.3 cm².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½

quiz.q: Three boxes are labelled Red, Blue and Mixed, and every label is wrong. From which box should you take one ball to fix all the labels?
quiz.explain: The box labelled Mixed cannot be mixed, so one ball tells you its true colour. Then the other two follow.
steps: Mixed label is wrong → that box is one colour
quiz.mistake: Picks a box whose ball would not decide the answer

quiz.q: In the box puzzle, you take a red ball from the box labelled Mixed. What does the box labelled Blue contain?
quiz.explain: The Mixed-labelled box is Red. The Blue-labelled box is not blue (its label is wrong) and not red (taken), so it is Mixed. The Red-labelled box is Blue.
steps: Box labelled Blue → not Blue, not Red → Mixed
quiz.mistake: Forgets that every label is wrong

teach.ask: Gappu sees a reed sticking 10 cm out of a pond. When he pulls its tip sideways 30 cm, it touches the water. How can he find the pond's depth?
teach.praise: d² + 900 = (d + 10)², so d = 40 cm! Bhaskara's lotus trick works for reeds too.
teach.nudge: If the depth is d, how long is the whole reed? Which side is the hypotenuse?

revise.summary: The theorem solves many puzzles: in the lotus problem d² + s² = (d + h)², a rhombus side comes from half-diagonals, and an equilateral triangle's altitude is (√3/2)a. Logic also helps in the wrong-label box puzzle.

Find a rhombus's side and perimeter from its diagonals
Find the altitude and area of an equilateral triangle
Solve the three-box puzzle with all labels wrong
remember: Lotus: d² + s² = (d + h)²
Rhombus side² = (half diagonal)² + (other half diagonal)²
Equilateral altitude h = (√3/2)a; area = ½ × a × h
Pick from the box labelled Mixed: it holds only one colour
traps: The depth is d, not the stem length d + h
Use half-diagonals, not full diagonals, for a rhombus
Don't forget that every label in the box puzzle is wrong
